reconcile.connective: Defenders deny any double-rejection: chapter 13 only forfeited the dynasty's perpetuation, while the personal rejection of Saul came only at the second transgression in chapter 15.

discrepancy.connective: The strongest objection is pressed by Julius Wellhausen, who read 1 Samuel's competing rejection accounts as conflated, mutually disagreeing traditions rather than one coherent sequence, so that chapters 13 and 15 stand as rival explanations of why Saul lost the kingdom.

skeptic.name: Julius Wellhausen
skeptic.work: Prolegomena to the History of Israel
skeptic.attribution: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (Eng. trans. 1885; Ger. Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels, 1883)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The non-continuance of the sovereignty is not to be regarded as a rejection, or as signifying that Saul had actually lost the throne so far as he himself was concerned … It was not till his second transgression that Saul was rejected, or declared unworthy of being king over the people of God (1 Samuel 15).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: K&D directly addresses the two-rejection tension: it denies that ch. 13 is a rejection at all (only a forfeiture of dynastic perpetuation) and locates the actual rejection of Saul in the second transgression of ch. 15, dissolving the 'two rejection events' claim. The two clauses are non-adjacent in the note but the ellipsis join preserves the author's argument.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on 1 Samuel 13:13-14 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this exact discrepancy at length on 1 Sam 13:13-14, arguing that the non-continuance of the dynasty in ch. 13 is not a rejection, and that Saul's actual rejection occurs only at the second transgression in ch. 15. (Haley's specific-passage coverage could not be confirmed, so a harmonizing commentator surfaced on the row and keyed to the passage is used instead.)
